summary: Torch MLP with moderate width, GELU and light weight decay on standardized raw features

data.title: Torch MLP with moderate width, GELU and light weight decay on standardized raw features
data.hypothesis: The map from 80 sensor-time temperatures to 4 conductivities is smooth but nonlinear (diffusion timescales scale like 1/k, so the mapping saturates). A 2-layer MLP with LayerNorm/AdamW should capture this nonlinearity better than linear models, and 3000 samples are enough for a 512x512 net when weight decay and early stopping are used.

author: ideator-neural
summary: PCA-denoised inputs into a deeper tapered MLP

data.title: PCA-denoised inputs into a deeper tapered MLP
data.hypothesis: Heat-equation sensor data are highly correlated across time (diffusion smooths everything), so most signal lives in a few dozen principal directions while sensor noise spreads over all 80. Projecting to 30 components removes noise and shrinks the input layer, which acts as regularisation for a tapered 512-256-128 network.

author: ideator-neural
summary: Log-feature MLP with tanh activation for smooth inverse map

data.title: Log-feature MLP with tanh activation for smooth inverse map
data.hypothesis: Temperatures decay roughly exponentially in time with rates proportional to the conductivities, so log temperatures are close to linear in k. That makes the regression easier, and a smooth tanh MLP with a lower learning rate fits a near-linear-plus-curvature map well. If the data contain negative or zero values the log transform may clip them, which this run will also reveal.

data.title: Kernel ridge (RBF) on log-temperatures, standardised

Log features linearise exponential decay rates, and an RBF kernel ridge with 3000 samples is a well-regularised smooth interpolant that should capture the remaining nonlinearity with low variance.

data.hypothesis: Conductivities are positive and the forward dependence is multiplicative (timescale ~ L^2/k), so regressing log k is better conditioned and errors are relative, matching rel_l2. config.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin
from sklearn.kernel_ridge import KernelRidge
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, KFold

class LogKRR(BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin):
    def __init__(self, seed=0):
        self.seed = seed
    def fit(self, X, y):
        y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
        # targets arrive standardised; shift to positive before log
        self.shift_ = -y.min(axis=0) + 1.0
        z = np.log(y + self.shift_)
        self.zm_ = z.mean(0); self.zs_ = z.std(0) + 1e-12
        zt = (z - self.zm_) / self.zs_
        d = X.shape[1]; v = X.var() + 1e-12
        base = 1.0 / (d * v)
        grid = {'alpha': [1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2], 'gamma': [base * g for g in (0.1, 0.3, 1.0)]}
        n = X.shape[0]
        idx = np.random.RandomState(self.seed).permutation(n)[:min(n, 1500)]
        gs = GridSearchCV(KernelRidge(kernel='rbf'), grid, cv=KFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=self.seed), scoring='neg_mean_squared_error')
        gs.fit(X[idx], zt[idx])
        self.model_ = KernelRidge(kernel='rbf', **gs.best_params_).fit(X, zt)
        return self
    def predict(self, X):
        z = self.model_.predict(X) * self.zs_ + self.zm_
        return np.exp(z) - self.shift_

def build_model(params, task, seed):
    return LogKRR(seed=seed)

author: ideator-ensembles
summary: Extra-trees on log temperatures with PCA denoising

data.title: Extra-trees on log temperatures with PCA denoising
data.hypothesis: The sensor time series are smooth and highly correlated, so PCA to about 20 components should strip most of the measurement noise while keeping the diffusion-rate information. Log features linearise the exponential decay modes, whose rates scale with the conductivities. Extra-trees averages randomised splits, which keeps variance low on 3000 samples and copes with the nonlinear k-to-u map.

author: ideator-ensembles
summary: Histogram GBM per conductivity segment on PCA-compressed features

data.title: Histogram GBM per conductivity segment on PCA-compressed features
data.hypothesis: Each conductivity mostly controls the local decay at nearby sensors, so each target depends on only a few features. Boosting finds these sparse interactions well. Fitting one booster per target with moderate depth, a slow learning rate and L2 regularisation should beat random forests on smooth targets. PCA to 24 components removes noise and speeds up fitting.

author: ideator-ensembles
summary: Kernel ridge on log features as the smooth-interpolant reference

data.title: Kernel ridge on log features as the smooth-interpolant reference
data.hypothesis: The parameter-to-observation map of the heat equation is smooth and low-dimensional (4 parameters), so an RBF interpolant on denoised log features can come close to the 0.05 target where piecewise-constant trees plateau. This tells us whether tree ensembles are approximation-limited. It is cheap at n=3000.

data.title: Ridge-then-boost residual stacking (custom)
data.hypothesis: In log space most of the inverse map is near-linear, because log-decay rates are roughly linear in log k. Trees approximate smooth linear trends poorly. Fitting ridge first and then boosting its residuals with gradient-boosted trees combines a globally smooth extrapolating base with a nonlinear correction. This should cut the staircase error of pure trees.

data.title: Log-temperature kernel ridge (spectral decay linearisation)
data.hypothesis: Diffusion data decays as a sum of exp(-lambda_j t) modes, and the eigenvalues lambda_j depend smoothly on the conductivities k. Taking logs turns the dominant late-time decay into near-linear trends in time. That makes the map from features to k smooth and low-curvature, which suits an RBF kernel ridge with 3000 samples.

author: ideator-domain
summary: Log-feature MLP for nonlinear inverse map

data.title: Log-feature MLP for nonlinear inverse map
data.hypothesis: The inverse map from sensor histories to the four segment conductivities is nonlinear: each sensor responds to several segments through harmonic-mean-like couplings. A moderately deep MLP on log temperatures can learn these interactions, and early stopping keeps it robust to measurement noise.

author: ideator-domain
summary: PLS on log temperatures (low-rank modal structure)

data.title: PLS on log temperatures (low-rank modal structure)
data.hypothesis: The 80 sensor-time values are strongly correlated because only a few diffusion modes survive past early times. PLS keeps the latent directions most predictive of k and discards the noise-dominated ones. It gives a fast, well-regularised near-linear baseline in log space.

author: ideator-domain
summary: Physics features (decay rates + inter-sensor log ratios) with kernel ridge

data.title: Physics features (decay rates + inter-sensor log ratios) with kernel ridge
data.hypothesis: Local conductivity shows up in two quantities. Temporal decay rates (d/dt log u per sensor) track the modal eigenvalues. Spatial log-ratios between adjacent sensors reflect the flux and gradient partition across segments. Supplying these explicitly, with signed raw values and log magnitudes, should make the inverse map much closer to linear and smooth for the RBF kernel. Because the sensor-time layout is unknown, both 4x20 and 20x4 orderings are encoded.

data.advice: All remaining ideas fit the objective and constraints. 1) Log features: noisy late-time temperatures can be near zero or negative, so use a fixed, documented floor such as log(max(u, eps)) with eps chosen on train only. Report how many values are clipped, or the log-feature results will be noise-dominated. 2) rel_l2 on positive k: regressing log k and exponentiating (idea-009) is well motivated. Consider applying the same log-target transform to the KRR and MLP ideas, and always compute rel_l2 in original k space. 3) idea-017 uses scaler=none with an RBF kernel on heterogeneous physics features. Standardise them, or the bandwidth will be dominated by one feature group. Compute finite-difference decay rates on smoothed or log-clipped signals, because differencing amplifies noise. 4) idea-009 and every gamma or alpha choice must be selected by CV on train or on val only. Keep the test split untouched until the single final evaluation. 5) Budget: 400 worker-seconds is tight for the MLPs (idea-002/003/004/015 at 200–300 epochs). Use early stopping on val, cap wall time per run, and prioritise KRR, ridge, PLS and idea-017 first, since they are cheap and likely closest to rel_l2 <= 0.05. 6) Fit scalers and PCA on train only. Fix the random seeds for the tree, boosting and MLP runs so their results can be compared.

summary: Log-target KRR with per-output (alpha, gamma) chosen by 3-fold CV on a stronger-regularisation grid

data.title: Log-target KRR with per-output (alpha, gamma) chosen by 3-fold CV on a stronger-regularisation grid
data.hypothesis: idea-009's log-target transform helps because the forward map is roughly exponential in conductivity. The parent idea-006 critique shows a large train/val gap (0.010 vs 0.035), so a grid that leans towards larger alpha and smaller bandwidth should cut variance. Choosing hyperparameters separately for each conductivity segment should help too, because segments far from the sensors are less identifiable and need more smoothing. Error is scored in the original target space, which matches rel_l2. One multi-output solve per fold keeps the cost low (9 combos x 3 folds on about 2000 samples).

config.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin
from sklearn.kernel_ridge import KernelRidge
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold

class LogKRRPerOutputCV(BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin):
    def __init__(self, alphas=(1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2), gmults=(0.15, 0.3, 0.5), seed=0):
        self.alphas = alphas
        self.gmults = gmults
        self.seed = seed

    def fit(self, X, y):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
        self.squeeze_ = (y.ndim == 1)
        if self.squeeze_:
            y = y[:, None]
        self.shift_ = -y.min(axis=0) + 1.0
        z = np.log(y + self.shift_)
        self.zm_ = z.mean(axis=0)
        self.zs_ = z.std(axis=0) + 1e-12
        zn = (z - self.zm_) / self.zs_
        base = 1.0 / (X.shape[1] * max(X.var(), 1e-12))
        combos = [(a, g) for a in self.alphas for g in self.gmults]
        err = np.zeros((len(combos), y.shape[1]))
        kf = KFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=self.seed)
        for tr, va in kf.split(X):
            for ci, (a, g) in enumerate(combos):
                m = KernelRidge(alpha=a, kernel='rbf', gamma=g * base).fit(X[tr], zn[tr])
                p = np.exp(m.predict(X[va]) * self.zs_ + self.zm_) - self.shift_
                err[ci] += np.sum((p - y[va]) ** 2, axis=0)
        best = err.argmin(axis=0)
        self.models_ = []
        for ci in np.unique(best):
            cols = np.where(best == ci)[0]
            a, g = combos[ci]
            m = KernelRidge(alpha=a, kernel='rbf', gamma=g * base).fit(X, zn[:, cols])
            self.models_.append((cols, m))
        self.n_out_ = y.shape[1]
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        zn = np.zeros((X.shape[0], self.n_out_))
        for cols, m in self.models_:
            p = m.predict(X)
            if p.ndim == 1:
                p = p[:, None]
            zn[:, cols] = p
        out = np.exp(zn * self.zs_ + self.zm_) - self.shift_
        return out[:, 0] if self.squeeze_ else out

def build_model(params, task, seed):
    return LogKRRPerOutputCV(seed=seed, **params)

summary: critic advice: None of the ideas violate constraints or leak test data. They all target the train/val overfitting gap seen in idea-006 and idea-015. Do mod

data.advice: None of the ideas violate constraints or leak test data. They all target the train/val overfitting gap seen in idea-006 and idea-015. Do model selection on train CV or val only. Notes: (1) idea-020 is listed as method 'custom' with empty params. Its implementation must explicitly define the alpha/gamma grid (lean toward larger alpha and smaller gamma_mult, e.g. alpha in [1e-3, 1e-1], gamma_mult in [0.05, 0.5]), fit one KRR per output on log(k), and exponentiate back before computing rel_l2. Run CV inside train only and use val to report. (2) SVR is single-output. Wrap it in MultiOutputRegressor and standardize the targets (ideally log-k), or epsilon and C will be badly mis-scaled. (3) The log-feature transform needs a clipping floor, since noisy late-time temperatures near the Dirichlet boundary can be non-positive. (4) idea-021 and idea-022 overlap. If budget is tight, keep idea-020, since its CV grid covers the idea-022 setting. (5) idea-018 (1024-512, 300 epochs) is the most expensive. Use early stopping on val to stay within the 400 worker-second budget. (6) Since several runs are near 0.027–0.035, the cheapest path to rel_l2 <= 0.05 robustness is to average the best KRR and best MLP predictions on val, which should cut variance further.

data.title: Log-feature tapered SiLU MLP with smaller batches and a lower peak LR
data.hypothesis: idea-018 and idea-019 added weight decay and width, and both did worse than idea-015. That suggests the inverse map is limited by optimisation, not overfitting. Batch 64 with lr=5e-4 over 300 cosine epochs gives more update steps and finer convergence near the optimum. Removing dropout and lowering weight decay to 3e-5 should cut the bias floor of the smooth inverse map, with early stopping on validation guarding against overfit. This tests whether the remaining error is regularisation bias.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin
from sklearn.kernel_ridge import KernelRidge

class MultiScaleLogKRR(BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin):
    def __init__(self, alpha=3e-3, gmults=(0.15, 0.3, 0.6), seed=0):
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.gmults = gmults
        self.seed = seed

    def fit(self, X, y):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
        if y.ndim == 1:
            y = y[:, None]
            self.flat_ = True
        else:
            self.flat_ = False
        self.shift_ = -y.min(axis=0) + 1.0
        z = np.log(y + self.shift_)
        self.zmean_ = z.mean(axis=0)
        zc = z - self.zmean_
        base = 1.0 / (X.shape[1] * max(X.var(), 1e-12))
        self.models_ = []
        for g in self.gmults:
            m = KernelRidge(alpha=self.alpha, kernel='rbf', gamma=g * base)
            m.fit(X, zc)
            self.models_.append(m)
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        zp = np.mean([m.predict(X) for m in self.models_], axis=0)
        if zp.ndim == 1:
            zp = zp[:, None]
        yp = np.exp(zp + self.zmean_) - self.shift_
        return yp.ravel() if self.flat_ else yp

def build_model(params, task, seed):
    return MultiScaleLogKRR(alpha=params.get('alpha', 3e-3), gmults=tuple(params.get('gmults', (0.15, 0.3, 0.6))), seed=seed)

data.title: Kernel ridge on sqrt-temperatures (alternative variance-stabilising transform)
data.hypothesis: The log transform linearises exponential modal decay, but it also amplifies noise at late times, where temperatures are near zero. A sqrt transform compresses the dynamic range more gently and may give a better signal-to-noise balance for the RBF metric. This tests whether the feature transform, rather than the target transform, is the bottleneck. This config is identical to idea-021 except for the feature transform (sqrt instead of log), so the comparison is direct: if it beats idea-021's 0.0276, a sqrt variant of the log-target KRR is the next step.

data.title: Log-feature KRR with robust scaling
data.hypothesis: Log-features of noisy near-zero late-time temperatures have heavy tails. Standard scaling lets those outliers set the bandwidth heuristic and the per-feature scale. Median/IQR scaling should keep the early-time informative channels from being down-weighted, improving the kernel metric at the same (alpha, gamma) as the best library KRR.

summary: Modal-truncation KRR: log features compressed to 24 PCA components

data.title: Modal-truncation KRR: log features compressed to 24 PCA components
data.hypothesis: The rod response is dominated by a few decaying eigenmodes per sensor, so the signal is roughly 4 sensors times about 6 modes. Truncating to 24 principal components should discard mostly noise directions. This is a harder truncation than the 40-component variant already proposed. It lets the RBF kernel use a more meaningful distance and should beat unreduced log-KRR at a similar compute cost.

data.advice: All six ideas are aligned, respect the constraints, and none touch the test split. Prioritise idea-026, the multi-bandwidth ensemble, and idea-029, the PCA-24 modal truncation. Both are cheap, low-risk extensions of the current best log-KRR. For idea-026, average the predictions in log-target space and then exponentiate, so it stays consistent with idea-009 and idea-020. Fix alpha in advance or select it on val only. idea-027 (sqrt) and idea-028 (robust scaler) are cheap single KRR fits, so run them. Note that the gamma_mult heuristic depends on the scaler, so a val sweep of gamma_mult in {0.15, 0.3, 0.6} is advisable for idea-028. The MLPs, idea-024 and idea-025, cost the most within the 400 worker-second budget on CPU. Cap epochs or use early stopping on val, and put them on separate workers. idea-024 runs 300 epochs at batch 64, which is about 14k steps; check that it fits the per-worker time slice before launching. If the KRR and MLP val predictions are complementary, a val-weighted blend of the best KRR and the best MLP is a reasonable next step. Report rel_l2 on val only. Touch test once, at the end.
